newsitem.title: USA: CBOT traders say USDA data bearish to winter wheat.
newsitem.headline: CBOT traders say USDA data bearish to winter wheat.

text.p: CBOT traders said data issued by USDA were bearish for winter wheat but neutral for corn and soybeans.
Soft red winter wheat futures were expected to open three to five cents a bushel lower.

Corn and soybeans were seen opening lower on almost ideal growing conditions in the Midwest with Friday's USDA reports producing few surprises. Corn was expected to open one to two cents a bushel lower and soybeans three to five cents down.
USDA put U.S. winter wheat production at 1.781 billion bushels. In a Reuter survey of analysts' the average projection was 1.687 billion.
"Winter wheat was bearish and we could be five cents lower in Chicago and Kansas City," a trader said.

U.S. other spring wheat production was, however, much lower than expected at 569 million bushels, versus an average analysts' estimate of 634 million. Durum output at 80 million was lower than an average analysts' estimate of 106 million.
"The spring wheat and durum numbers were shockingly low and bullish," a trader said.
USDA put the Kansas wheat crop at 449 million bushels, the state's largest crop since the record 472 million harvest in 1990.
Analysts said USDA's monthly supply/demand report produced few surprises.

USDA put 1997/98 wheat ending stocks at 650 million bushels, in line with forecasts of 600 to 700 million, while soybean 1997/98 ending stocks at 285 million was also within the 280 to 300 million bushel range of trade estimates.
Corn ending stocks for 1997/98 were also much as expected at 1.196 million bushels.

"I don't think there were any huge surprises. In the near-term weather is going to be the dominant factor," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities, noting favorable conditions for growing corn and soybeans in the U.S. Midwest should lead to a lower CBOT opening Friday.
